slides.title: Unit Outline
slides.body:
Unit Outline

Part 1: Neuronal Signalling
Part 2: Ion Channels and the Resting Membrane Potential
Part 3: Generation of an Action Potential
Part 4: Propagation of Action Potentials
Part 5: Neurotransmission

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes: In this unit, we will begin by discussing neural signalling in general, and then we will turn to discussions of membrane potentials – the voltage differences across the membrane. Within those parts, we will look at how resting membrane potentials are generated and maintained, and then we will turn to the generation, and then propagation, of action potentials. Finally, we will conclude with a section on neurotransmission.

Part 1: Neuronal Signalling

Before diving into detail, let’s examine a scenario that both reviews and introduces some new terms:
1. Sensory neurons in the skin sense a stimulus – here, water temperature. The strength of the neural signal that starts here is dependent on the strength of the stimulus.

Testing the Water.

2. The graded potential from the sensory endings, if strong enough, will initiate an action potential at the initial segment of the axon (which is immediately adjacent to the sensory endings in the skin).

Testing the Water.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024

slides.body:
Part 1: Neuronal Signalling

4. An action potential is initiated at the axon hillock of this neuron and travels up the sensory pathway to a region of the brain called the thalamus (relay station). Another synapse passes the information along to the next neuron.

Testing the Water.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes: 4. An action potential is initiated at the axon hillock of this neuron and travels up the sensory pathway to a region of the brain called the thalamus, the part of the central nervous system that acts as a relay for sensory information. Another synapse passes the information along to the next neuron.

slides.title: Part 1: Neuronal Signalling
slides.body:
Part 1: Neuronal Signalling

5. The sensory pathway ends when the signal reaches the cerebral cortex. 
conscious perception now possible
information here is processed among many neurons, integrating the stimulus of the water temperature with your emotional state, memories, etc.

Testing the Water.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes: 5. The thalamus then sends the sensory information to the cerebral cortex, the outermost layer of grey matter in the brain, where conscious perception of that water temperature begins. Within the cerebral cortex, information is processed among many neurons, integrating the stimulus of the water temperature with other sensory stimuli, with your emotional state (you are sleepy and a cold shower could help wake you up), memories (cold showers can be a bit rough). Finally, a plan is developed about what to do, whether that is to turn the temperature up or down. To do any of these things, the cerebral cortex has to send a command out to your body to move muscles. The sensory pathway ends when the signal reaches the cerebral cortex.

Part 1: Neuronal Signalling

6. After integration with neurons in other parts of the cerebral cortex, a motor command is sent from the precentral gyrus of the frontal cortex (primary motor cortex).

Testing the Water.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024

slides.body:
Part 1: Neuronal Signalling

7. The upper motor neuron sends an action potential down to the spinal cord. The target of the upper motor neuron is the dendrites of the lower motor neuron in the grey matter of the spinal cord.

Testing the Water.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes: 7. The upper motor neurons in the primary motor cortex have axons that extend all the way down the spinal cord. At the level of the spinal cord at which these axons makes synapses, a graded potential occurs in the cell membrane of a lower motor neuron. This second motor neuron is responsible for causing muscle fibres to contract. In the manner described in the unit on muscle tissue, an action potential travels along the motor neuron axon into the periphery.

muscles can then turn temperature warmer or colder or withdraw hand

Testing the Water.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes: 8. The axon of the lower motor neuron emerges from the spinal cord in a nerve and connects to a muscle through a neuromuscular junction to cause contraction of the target muscle. Acetylcholine is released at this specialized synapse.

slides.title: Part 1: Neuronal Signalling
slides.body:
Part 1: Neuronal Signalling

Okay, now let’s look at some more details…
thermal stimuli were transduced by thermoreceptors into electrical signals
the cell membrane of the thermoreceptors changes its electrical state (voltage).
amount of change depends on strength of stimulus (how hot the water is) – this is a graded potential 
a sufficient stimulus changes the voltage of the cell membrane enough to meet a threshold and generate an action potential that will travel (propagate) down the axon

The Sensory Input. Receptors in the skin sense the temperature of the water.

Graded potentials.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes: Okay, let’s look at some of these components in more detail. The initial sensory stimulus of temperature was transduced by a thermoreceptor into an electrical signal. The cell membrane of the thermoreceptors changes its electrical state (that is, its voltage). The amount of change is dependent on the strength of the stimulus (how hot the water is). This is called a graded potential. If the stimulus is strong, the voltage of the cell membrane will change enough to meet a threshold and generate an action potential that will travel (propagate) down the axon.

slides.title: Part 1: Neuronal Signalling
slides.body:
Part 1: Neuronal Signalling

Action potential propagates along axon 
from the axon hillock to the axon terminals and into the synaptic end bulbs 
it causes the release of neurotransmitters into synapse - diffuse to receptors on postsynaptic neuron
new graded potential begins in postsynaptic neuron – if sufficient, can generate action potential

Chemical synapse. Credit: user:Looie496 created file; Illustrator: Christy Krames, MA, CMI, for US National Institutes of Health, National Institute on Aging, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
The action potential propagates along the axon from the axon hillock to the axon terminals and into the synaptic end bulbs. When this signal reaches the end bulbs, it causes the release of neurotransmitters into a synapse.

The neurotransmitter diffuses across the short distance of the synapse and binds to a receptor protein of the postsynaptic neuron. When the molecular signal binds to the receptor, the cell membrane of the target neuron changes its electrical state and a new graded potential begins. If that graded potential is strong enough to reach threshold, the second neuron generates an action potential at its own axon hillock.

slides.title: Part 1: Neuronal Signalling
slides.body:
Part 1: Neuronal Signalling

Lower motor neurons release ACh onto motor end plate at the neuromuscular junction
Opening of nicotinic receptor channels causes end plate potential 
large depolarization of voltage due to neuromuscular junction being very large synapse
causes muscle fibres contract
Regular synapses are much smaller and require multiple neurotransmitter release events to cause sufficient depolarization to reach an action potential threshold

Regular synapse. Credit: Laboratoires Servier, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Neuromuscular junction. Credit: Laboratoires Servier, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Opening of nicotinic receptor channels by acetylcholine causes a large potential known as an end plate potential. This change in voltage is extra large, due to the neuromuscular junction being a very large synapse. When the lower motor neuron excites the muscle fibre, it contracts. All of this occurs in a fraction of a second. 

Okay, now let’s move on and look at some of these steps at a cellular and molecular level.

slides.title: Part 2: Ion Channels and the Resting Membrane Potential
slides.body:
Part 2: Ion Channels and the Resting Membrane Potential

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes: So on to Part 2: Ion Channels and the Resting Membrane Potential.

slides.title: Part 2: Ion Channels and the Resting Membrane Potential
slides.body:
Part 2: Ion Channels and the Resting Membrane Potential

An excitable membrane is basis of graded and action potentials
most body cells use ions to build up charge across cell membrane
ions are charged and thus need ion channels or transport pumps to pass through phospholipid bilayer of membrane

Cell Membrane and Transmembrane Proteins. The cell membrane is composed of a phospholipid bilayer and has many transmembrane proteins, including different types of channel proteins that serve as ion channels.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
We now need to discuss the role of the excitable membrane in generating the graded and action potentials that we just discussed. We will use an action potential as the model for our discussion.

Most cells in the body make use of charged particles (ions) to build up a charge across the cell membrane. Cells make use of the cell membrane to regulate ion movement between the extracellular fluid and cytosol. As you learned in the unit on cell membranes, the cell membrane is primarily responsible for regulating what can cross the membrane and what stays on only one side. The cell membrane is a phospholipid bilayer, so only substances that can pass directly through the hydrophobic core can diffuse through unaided. Charged particles, which are hydrophilic by definition, cannot pass through the cell membrane without assistance. Transmembrane proteins, specifically channel proteins, make this possible. Several passive ion channels, as well as active transport pumps, are necessary to generate a transmembrane potential and an action potential. Ion channels are pores that allow specific charged particles to cross the membrane in response to an existing concentration gradient.

slides.title: Part 2: Ion Channels and the Resting Membrane Potential
slides.body:
Part 2: Ion Channels and the Resting Membrane Potential

Sodium-potassium pump (ATPase) uses ATP hydrolysis to move Na+ out and K+ into cell
Na+ ion channels allow Na+ to diffuse in, depolarizing cell
K+ ion channels allow K+ to diffuse out, hyperpolarizing cell

Sodium-potassium pump and ion channels. Credit: Blausen.com staff (2014). "Medical gallery of Blausen Medical 2014". WikiJournal of Medicine 1 (2). DOI:10.15347/wjm/2014.010. ISSN 2002-4436.Derivative by Mikael Häggström, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Recall that the sodium/potassium pump moves sodium ions out of a cell and potassium ions into a cell, thus regulating ion concentration on both sides of the cell membrane. The sodium/potassium pump requires energy in the form of adenosine triphosphate (ATP), so it is also referred to as an ATPase. As was explained in the cell chapter, the concentration of sodium ions is higher outside the cell than inside, and the concentration of potassium ions is higher inside the cell than outside. That means that this pump is moving the ions against the concentration gradients for sodium and potassium, which is why it requires energy. In fact, the pump basically maintains those concentration gradients.

If open, Na+ ion channels allow Na+ to diffuse in, depolarizing the cell, while K+ ions channels allow K+ to diffuse out, hyperpolarizing the cell.

slides.title: Part 2: Ion Channels and the Resting Membrane Potential
slides.body:
Part 2: Ion Channels and the Resting Membrane Potential

Most ion channels are gated
ligand-gated channel opens when particular molecule (a ligand) binds to receptor on extracellular region of the channel
also known as ionotropic receptor because allows ions to cross the membrane, changing its charge

Ligand-Gated Channels. When the ligand, in this case the neurotransmitter acetylcholine, binds to a specific location on the extracellular surface of the channel protein, the pore opens to allow select ions through. The ions, in this case, are cations of sodium, calcium, and potassium.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
However, most ion channels are gated and thus do not always freely allow ions to diffuse across the membrane. 

A ligand-gated channel opens because a signaling molecule, a ligand, binds to a receptor on the extracellular region of the channel. This type of channel is also known as an ionotropic receptor because when the ligand, known as a neurotransmitter in the nervous system, binds to the protein, ions cross the membrane changing its charge.

slides.title: Part 2: Ion Channels and the Resting Membrane Potential
slides.body:
Part 2: Ion Channels and the Resting Membrane Potential

Most ion channels are gated
a mechanoreceptor opens with a physical distortion of the cell membrane
e.g., touch receptors
thermoreceptors work in a similar way, as temperature changes affect the protein structure, which physically opens the channel

Mechanically Gated Channels. When a mechanical change occurs in the surrounding tissue, such as pressure or touch, the channel is physically opened. Thermoreceptors work on a similar principle. When the local tissue temperature changes, the protein reacts by physically opening the channel.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
A mechanoreceptor is a mechanically gated channel that opens because of a physical distortion of the cell membrane. Many channels associated with the sense of touch are mechanically gated. For example, as pressure is applied to the skin, these channels open and allow ions to enter the cell. 

Thermoreceptors work in a similar way, as when the local tissue temperature changes, the protein reacts by physically opening the channel.

slides.title: Part 2: Ion Channels and the Resting Membrane Potential
slides.body:
Part 2: Ion Channels and the Resting Membrane Potential

Most ion channels are gated
a voltage-gated channel responds to voltage changes in the membrane
normally inside is negative relative to outside (a negative voltage)
most voltage-gated channels open when inside becomes less negative, or even positive, relative to the outside

+

+

+

+

+

+

+

+

Voltage-Gated Potassium Channels. Voltage-gated channels open when the transmembrane voltage changes around them. Amino acids in the structure of the protein are sensitive to charge and cause the pore to open to the selected ion. Adapted from OpenStax by David Kabelik.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes: A voltage-gated channel is a channel that responds to changes in the electrical properties of the membrane in which it is embedded. Normally, the inner portion of the membrane is at a negative voltage. When that voltage becomes less negative, the channel begins to allow ions to cross the membrane.

slides.title: Part 2: Ion Channels and the Resting Membrane Potential
slides.body:
Part 2: Ion Channels and the Resting Membrane Potential

However, a leakage channel (or leak channel) is randomly gated – it opens and closes at random, hence allowing a steady leakage of ions across
leaky K+ channels contribute to resting membrane potential (voltage)

Leakage Channels. In certain situations, ions need to move across the membrane randomly. The particular electrical properties of certain cells are modified by the presence of this type of channel.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
A leakage channel (or leak channel) is randomly gated, meaning that it opens and closes at random, hence allowing a steady leakage of ions across the membrane. There is no actual event that opens the channel; instead, it has an intrinsic rate of switching between the open and closed states. Leakage channels contribute to the resting transmembrane voltage of the excitable membrane.

The primary leak channel in cells is a leaky potassium channel. When the positively charged potassium cations leave the cell, they make the area outside of the membrane more positive with their charge, and leave the inside more negative then when they were present. Hence, the inside of a cell is usually more negative than the outside.

slides.title: Part 2: Ion Channels and the Resting Membrane Potential
slides.body:
Part 2: Ion Channels and the Resting Membrane Potential

Membrane Potential
measure inside relative to outside, in mV
cells vary, but on average, resting membrane voltage is -70 mV
primarily driven by K+ leaking out, slightly opposed by tiny trickle of Na+ leaking in

Measuring Charge across a Membrane with a Voltmeter. A recording electrode is inserted into the cell and a reference electrode is outside the cell. By comparing the charge measured by these two electrodes, the transmembrane voltage is determined. It is conventional to express that value for the cytosol relative to the outside.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
The membrane potential, or distribution of charge across the cell membrane, is measured in millivolts. The standard is to compare the inside of the cell relative to the outside, so the membrane potential is a value representing the charge on the intracellular side relative to the outside.

With the ions distributed across the membrane at these concentrations, the difference in charge is measured at -70 mV, the value described as the resting membrane potential. The exact value measured for the resting membrane potential varies between cells, but -70 mV is the most commonly recorded value. This voltage is driven by some important proteins in the membrane. Potassium leakage channels allow K+ to slowly move out of the cells. To a much lesser extent, sodium leakage channels allow Na+ to slowly move into the cell. The constant activity of the Na+/K+ pump maintains the ion gradients. This may appear to be a waste of energy, but each has a role in maintaining the membrane potential.

slides.title: Part 2: Ion Channels and the Resting Membrane Potential
slides.body:
Part 2: Ion Channels and the Resting Membrane Potential

The concentration of ions in extracellular and intracellular fluids is largely balanced, with a net neutral charge
at rest, a slight difference solely exists right at the membrane surface due to K+ leak channels

Electrical charges across cell membrane. Credit: David Kabelik, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Note that the concentration of ions in extracellular and intracellular fluids is largely balanced, with a net neutral charge. It is solely a slight difference in charge that occurs right at the membrane surface, both internally and externally, which we detect as a voltage difference – hence, we refer to it as “at the membrane”. It is the difference in this very limited region that has all the power in neurons (and muscle cells) to generate electrical signals, including action potentials.

When the cell is at rest, and the ion channels are closed (except for leakage channels), ions are distributed across the membrane in a very predictable way. The concentration of Na+ outside the cell is 10 times greater than the concentration inside. Also, the concentration of K+ inside the cell is greater than outside. The cytosol contains a high concentration of anions, in the form of phosphate ions and negatively charged proteins. Large anions are also a component of the inner cell membrane. Meanwhile, the extracellular fluid also has a high concentration of Cl-, which helps to balance the extracellular charge.

Part 3: Generation of an Action Potential

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes: Now let’s turn to Part 3: Generation of an Action Potential.

slides.title: Part 3: Generation of an Action Potential
slides.body:
Part 3: Generation of an Action Potential

To generate an electrical signal, membrane potential (V) must change
graded potentials (usually in dendrites of neuron) are changes in membrane V whose size depends on intensity of stimulus (e.g., was the shower warm or hot)
depolarizing stimuli bring V higher (usually via Na+ or Ca2+ influx)
hyperpolarizing stimuli bring V lower (usually via Cl- influx or K+ efflux)

Graded Potentials. Graded potentials are temporary changes in the membrane voltage, the characteristics of which depend on the size of the stimulus. Some types of stimuli cause depolarization of the membrane, whereas others cause hyperpolarization. It depends on the specific ion channels that are activated in the cell membrane.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
A resting membrane potential describes the steady state of the cell, which is a dynamic process that is balanced by ion leakage and ion pumping. Without any outside influence, it will not change. To get an electrical signal started, the membrane potential thus has to change.

As mentioned earlier, local changes in the membrane potential are called graded potentials and these are usually associated with the dendrites of a neuron. The amount of change in the membrane potential is determined by the size of the stimulus that causes it. In the example of testing the temperature of the shower, slightly warm water would only initiate a small change in a thermoreceptor, whereas hot water would cause a large amount of change in the membrane potential.

Graded potentials can be of two sorts, either they are depolarizing or hyperpolarizing. For a membrane at the resting potential, a graded potential represents a change in that voltage either above or below -70 mV. Depolarizing graded potentials are often the result of Na+ or Ca2+ entering the cell. Both of these ions have higher concentrations outside the cell than inside and are driven inward by those concentration gradients, as well as due to their attraction to the negative charge near the inner membrane. Because Na+ or Ca2+ have a positive charge, when they move into the cell, they cause the inside to become somewhat less negative relative to the outside. Hyperpolarizing graded potentials can be caused by K+ leaving the cell, taking their positive charge out of the cell, or Cl– entering the cell, bringing in a negative charge. Thus, if a positive charge moves out of a cell, the cell becomes more negative; if a negative charge enters the cell, the same thing happens.

slides.title: Part 3: Generation of an Action Potential
slides.body:
Part 3: Generation of an Action Potential

Action potentials are “all or none” because they either occur and change the membrane voltage a given amount (not graded), or they do not occur at all

Action potential spikes. Adapted from: William M. Connelly, Vincenzo Crunelli, and Adam C. Errington, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes: Action potentials, on the other hand are described as “all or none” because they either occur and change the membrane voltage a given amount (not graded), or they do not occur at all.

slides.title: Part 3: Generation of an Action Potential
slides.body:
Part 3: Generation of an Action Potential

Action potentials are “all or none” 
stronger stimuli will affect frequency, not amplitude
will initiate multiple action potentials more quickly, but the individual signals are not bigger

Action potential frequency. Adapted from: Drpaulineneveu, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes: Action potentials are “all or none.” Either the membrane reaches the threshold and everything occurs as described above, or the membrane does not reach the threshold and nothing else happens. All action potentials peak at the same voltage (+30 mV), so one action potential is not bigger than another. Stronger stimuli will initiate multiple action potentials more quickly, but the individual signals are not bigger. Thus, for example, you will not feel a greater sensation of pain, or have a stronger muscle contraction, because of the size of the action potential because they are not different sizes.

slides.title: Part 3: Generation of an Action Potential
slides.body:
Part 3: Generation of an Action Potential

Action potential begins at axon hillock if graded potential from dendrites & soma if of sufficient depolarizing magnitude
opens voltage-gated Na+ channels
Na+ ions enter, due to concentration gradient, and electrical gradient (attraction to inner negative charge)
depolarization from Na+ influx spreads to adjacent axonal segments, opens channels there, etc.

Action potential initiation. Adapted from: Helixitta, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Action potentials start at a neuron’s axon hillock, or near the motor end plate of a skeletal muscle, with sodium channels opening in the membrane. This occurs if the graded potential arriving from the dendrites and cell soma is of sufficient depolarizing magnitude to open these voltage-gated sodium channels. The graded potential itself started at other types of channels, usually ligand-gated channels that were opened by neurotransmitters binding to those receptor-channels at the dendrites.

Because the concentration of Na+ is higher outside the cell than inside the cell by a factor of 10, ions will rush into the cell, driven largely by the concentration gradient, but again, also by the electrical gradient across the membrane. Because sodium is a positively charged ion, it will change the relative voltage immediately inside the cell relative to immediately outside. The resting potential is the state of the membrane at a voltage of -70 mV, so the sodium cation entering the cell will cause it to become less negative. This is known as depolarization, meaning the membrane potential moves toward zero.

slides.title: Part 3: Generation of an Action Potential
slides.body:
Part 3: Generation of an Action Potential

Concentration gradient for Na+ is so strong that it will continue to enter the cell even after the membrane potential has become zero, so that the voltage immediately around the pore begins to become positive

depolarization due to Na+ influx

depolarization due to graded potential
from dendrites & cell soma

AP threshold   
     (opens V-gated 
     Na+ channels)

Graph of Action Potential. Plotting voltage measured across the cell membrane against time, the action potential begins with depolarization, followed by repolarization, which goes past the resting potential into hyperpolarization, and finally the membrane returns to rest.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes: You can see a depolarization on this figure. The concentration gradient for Na+ is so strong that it will continue to enter the cell even after the membrane potential has become zero, so that the voltage immediately around the pore begins to become positive. The electrical gradient also plays a role, as negative proteins below the membrane attract the sodium ion. The membrane potential will reach +30 mV by the time sodium ions have fully entered the cell.

slides.title: Part 3: Generation of an Action Potential
slides.body:
Part 3: Generation of an Action Potential

Na+ channels become inactivated at positive membrane voltage, preventing further depolarization 
(at that segment of membrane – remember that the depolarization does spread)
resets to just regular “closed” at resting membrane voltage

these become inactivated

these open next

Sodium channels open then inactivate. Credit: Tryptofish, adapted by David Kabelik, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Action potential initiation. Adapted from: Helixitta, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes: As the membrane potential reaches +30 mV, the sodium channels become inactivated, preventing further entry of sodium ions. These channels will stop being inactivated later, when the cell is back at it’s resting membrane voltage, at which time they will again be closed and ready to reopen following the arrival of the next graded potential. However, until the cell membrane’s voltage drops, these channels remain inactivated (rather than closed), and thus cannot be used to allow any more sodium ions to enter the cell, even if another depolarizing graded potential arrives.

slides.title: Part 3: Generation of an Action Potential
slides.body:
Part 3: Generation of an Action Potential

K+ leak channels are always active and thus not shown here

K+ channels open
K+ ions leave (repolarization) cell according to concentration gradient and electrical gradient (inner positivity repels them)
restores inner voltage to negative value
sometimes even undershoot, before K+ channels close and balance restored

V-gated  Na+ channel

Na+

K+

V-gated  K+ channel

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024

Action potential channels. Credit: CThompson02, adapted by David Kabelik, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
slides.notes:
Next, potassium channels open. A concentration gradient drives the K+ outward, and now that the inside of the cell is temporarily more positive than the outside (at +30 mV), an electrical gradient drives them outward as well. As K+ start to leave the cell, taking their positive charges with them, the membrane potential begins to move back toward its resting voltage. This is called repolarization, meaning that the membrane voltage moves back toward the -70 mV value of the resting membrane potential.

Repolarization returns the membrane potential to the -70 mV value that indicates the resting potential, but it actually overshoots that value. Potassium ions reach equilibrium when the membrane voltage is below -70 mV, so a period of hyperpolarization occurs while the K+ channels are open. Those K+ channels are slightly delayed in closing, accounting for this undershoot (of voltage).

slides.title: Part 4: Propagation of Action Potentials
slides.body:
Part 4: Propagation of Action Potentials

Action potential starts at axon hillock – possesses high density of voltage-gated Na+ channels
depolarization from Na+ influx spreads to next segment, opening more V-gated Na+ channels
Na+ channels of initial segment then inactivated - until repolarized and closed, these channels are blocked
this initial segment of membrane is thus in a refractory period – depolarization flowing backward from next segment fizzles out (no backward-spreading APs!)
K+ channels then open to repolarize this initial segment

Propagation of an Action Potential Along an Unmyelinated Axon.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
The action potential is initiated at the beginning of the axon, at the axon hillock. There is a high density of voltage-gated Na+ channels so that rapid depolarization can take place here. Going down the length of the axon, the action potential is propagated because more voltage-gated Na+ channels are opened as the depolarization spreads. This spreading occurs because Na+ enters through the channel and moves along the inside of the cell membrane. As the depolarization spreads, new voltage-gated Na+ channels open and more ions rush into the cell, spreading the depolarization a little farther.

Because voltage-gated Na+ channels are inactivated at the peak of the depolarization (by the inactivation gate), they cannot be opened again for a brief time—the absolute refractory period. Because of this, depolarization spreading back toward previously opened channels has no effect. The action potential must propagate toward the axon terminals; as a result, the polarity of the neuron is maintained, as mentioned above.

slides.title: Part 4: Propagation of Action Potentials
slides.body:
Part 4: Propagation of Action Potentials

Unmyelinated neurons – APs spread from segment to adjacent segment to adjacent segment
depolarization regenerated at each segment
this process is slow:
opening up channels in each segment takes time
ion influx and spread takes time
But without regeneration, the signal would fade – this type of “wire” isn’t “insulated”

Action potential would spread as graded potential, and thus fade, without continuous regeneration

Fading of graded potential if action potential was not regenerated. Adapted by: David Kabelik, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Note that that last neuron was unmyelinated, so the action potential spread from segment to adjacent segment to adjacent segment, all the way down to axon terminus. Opening up channels in each segment takes time, as does waiting for cations to flow in across the membrane, and spread their charge. This process can be sped up via myelination.

However, without regeneration at each adjacent segment of membrane, the depolarization would fade. You can think of unmyelinated neurons as uninsulated wires, where the signal fades over distance, and thus needs to keep being regenerated. A way to speed up action potentials is thus to “insulate” the axon of the neuron—and this is where myelin comes in.

slides.title: Part 4: Propagation of Action Potentials
slides.body:
Part 4: Propagation of Action Potentials

Myelinated neurons – depolarization spreads through myelinated segments without fading too much (“insulated”)
does not need to regenerate the signal until next Node of Ranvier (where next set of Na+ channels are present)
infrequent regenerations = greater speed

Propagation of an Action Potential Along a Myelinated Axon. Nodes of Ranvier are gaps in myelin coverage along axons. Nodes contain voltage-gated K+ and Na+ channels. Action potentials travel down the axon by jumping from one node to the next. This diagram shows the nodes of Ranvier and the internodal (myelinated) segments with approximately the same length. This is not accurate: in real axons, the segments with myelin are about one thousand times longer than the nodes!

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes: When myelination is present, the action potential propagates differently. Sodium ions that enter the cell at the initial segment start to spread along the length of the axon segment, but there are no voltage-gated Na+ channels until the first node of Ranvier. Because there is not constant opening of these channels along the axon segment, the depolarization spreads at a much faster speed. The distance between nodes (1-3 mm) means that the membrane is still sufficiently depolarized (above threshold) by the time it reaches the next node. As Na+ spreads along the inside of the membrane of the axon segment, the charge starts to dissipate, but the myelin “insulation” keeps it from dissipating too quickly. If the node were any farther down the axon, that depolarization may have fallen off too much for voltage-gated Na+ channels to be activated at the next node of Ranvier.

slides.title: Part 4: Propagation of Action Potentials
slides.body:
Part 4: Propagation of Action Potentials

Myelinated segments are ~1000X longer than nodes of Ranvier
“jumping over” these myelinated segments is called saltatory conduction
dramatically increases speed of action potential over unmyelinated continuous conduction

Action potential speed in unmyelinated and myelinated neurons. Credit: Dr. Jana, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes: Propagation along an unmyelinated axon is referred to as continuous conduction; along the length of a myelinated axon, it is saltatory conduction. Continuous conduction is slow because there are always voltage-gated Na+ channels opening, and more and more Na+ are rushing into the cell. Saltatory conduction is faster because the action potential basically jumps from one node to the next (saltare means “to leap”), and the new influx of Na+ renews the depolarized membrane.

slides.title: Part 4: Propagation of Action Potentials
slides.body:
Part 4: Propagation of Action Potentials

Diameter of axon also influences speed of action potential
wider axons encounter less resistance to spread of charge down axon

Propagation of an action potential along an unmyelinated axons of varying diameters. Adapted by: David Kabelik, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes: Along with the myelination of the axon, the diameter of the axon can influence the speed of conduction. Much as water runs faster in a wide river than in a narrow creek, Na+-based depolarization spreads faster down a wide axon than down a narrow one. This concept is known as resistance and is generally true for electrical wires or plumbing, just as it is true for axons, although the specific conditions are different at the scales of electrons or ions versus water in a river.

slides.title: Part 5: Neurotransmission
slides.body:
Part 5: Neurotransmission

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes: Now let’s finish up with Part 5: Neurotransmission.

slides.title: Part 5: Neurotransmission
slides.body:
Part 5: Neurotransmission

Depolarization spreads, from synapse to axon hillock, as a graded potential
decreases in magnitude as it spreads, so only sufficient (or combined = summation) depolarizations reach action potential threshold

Chemical synapse. Credit: user:Looie496 created file; Illustrator: Christy Krames, MA, CMI, for US National Institutes of Health, National Institute on Aging, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
As we said previously, action potentials are all or none. Once they are initiated via a depolarization meeting the threshold voltage of sodium channels at the axon hillock, they run on their own, regenerating down the axon. The question is thus, “What causes the depolarization that triggers these action potentials?” 

Temporary changes to the cell membrane voltage can result from neurons receiving information from the environment, or from the action of one neuron on another. These special types of potentials influence a neuron and determine whether an action potential will occur or not. Many of these transient signals originate at the synapse, the connection between electrically active cells, and then travel to the axon hillock as a graded potential. Because the magnitude of graded potentials decreases as they spread, only sufficient (or combined) depolarizations reach the action potential threshold by the time the signal reaches the axon hillock.

slides.title: Part 5: Neurotransmission
slides.body:
Part 5: Neurotransmission

Chemical synapses
neurotransmitter carries signal between neurons
Electrical synapses
graded potential passes via gap junctions from neuron to neuron

Chemical synapse. Credit: vectorization: Mouagip (talk)Synapse_diag1.png: Drawn by fr:Utilisateur:DakeCorrections of original PNG by en:User:Nrets This W3C-unspecified vector image was created with Adobe Illustrator., CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Electrical synapse. Credit: Drawn by  DakeCorrections, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes: There are two types of synapses: chemical synapses and electrical synapses. In a chemical synapse, a chemical signal—namely, a neurotransmitter—is released from one cell and it affects the other cell. In an electrical synapse, there is a direct connection between the two cells so that ions can pass directly from one cell to the next. If one cell is depolarized in an electrical synapse, the joined cell also depolarizes because the ions pass between the cells. Chemical synapses involve the transmission of chemical information from one cell to the next. This section will concentrate on the chemical type of synapse.

slides.title: Part 5: Neurotransmission
slides.body:
Part 5: Neurotransmission

Chemical synaptic transmission:
action potential reaches axon terminal
depolarization causes voltage-gated Ca2+ channels in the membrane of the synaptic end bulb to open
Ca2+ ions associate with proteins of vesicles facilitating their merging with presynaptic membrane
neurotransmitter released through exocytosis into synaptic cleft
neurotransmitter diffuses to postsynaptic membrane – binds to its specific receptor
opens channels causing depolarization or hyperpolarization of postsynaptic cell membrane
leads to excitation of postsynaptic cell (and possibly generation of action potential) or inhibition
neurotransmitter is removed from synaptic cleft by diffusion, by enzymes that break it down chemically, or by transporters in presynaptic cell membrane

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024

Synaptic Transmission. The pre-synaptic neuron signals a postsynaptic neuron by releasing neurotransmitter across the synaptic cleft.
slides.notes:
Chemical synaptic transmission (or neurotransmission) takes place through the following steps:

An action potential reaches the axon terminal.
The change in voltage causes voltage-gated Ca2+ channels in the membrane of the synaptic end bulb to open.
The concentration of Ca2+ increases inside the end bulb, and Ca2+ associate with proteins in the outer surface of neurotransmitter vesicles facilitating the merging of the vesicle with the presynaptic membrane. The neurotransmitter is then released through exocytosis into the small gap between the cells, known as the synaptic cleft.
Once in the synaptic cleft, the neurotransmitter diffuses the short distance to the postsynaptic membrane and can interact with neurotransmitter receptors. Receptors are specific for the neurotransmitter, and the two fit together like a key and lock. One neurotransmitter binds to its receptor and will not bind to receptors for other neurotransmitters, making the binding a specific chemical event.
The interaction of the neurotransmitter with the receptor can result in depolarization or hyperpolarization of the postsynaptic cell membrane, leading to excitation of the postsynaptic cell (and possibly the generation of a new action potential) or inhibition, respectively.
The neurotransmitter is removed from the synaptic cleft by diffusion, due to the action of enzymes that break it down chemically, or by transporters in the presynaptic cell membrane.

slides.title: Part 5: Neurotransmission
slides.body:
Part 5: Neurotransmission

Neurotransmitter systems
amino acids: 
glutamate (excitatory)
GABA (gamma-aminobutyric acid, inhibitory, in brain)
glycine (inhibitory, in spinal cord)
biogenic amines (made from amino acids):
serotonin (made from tryptophan)
dopamine, norepinephrine, and epinephrine (the catecholamines, made from tyrosine)
cholinergic system: 
acetylcholine (neuromuscular junction, autonomic nervous system, throughout the brain)
neuropeptides (often released at synapses in combination with another neurotransmitter):
met-enkephalin and beta-endorphin (endogenous opioids – analgesic and pleasure-inducing)
oxytocin, vasopressin (anti-diuretic hormone)

Examples of Neurotransmitters. Shown are some examples of major transmitters, their chemical structures and some of their functions.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
There are several systems of neurotransmitters that are found at various synapses in the nervous system. Some important examples include the following:

Amino acids: This includes glutamate, the main excitatory neurotransmitter in the central nervous system, GABA (gamma-aminobutyric acid), the main inhibitory neurotransmitter in the brain and glycine, the main inhibitory neurotransmitter in the spinal cord.

Biogenic amines: This is a group of neurotransmitters that are enzymatically made from amino acids. For example, the neurotransmitter serotonin is made from tryptophan. Other biogenic amines are made from tyrosine, and include the catecholamines dopamine, norepinephrine, and epinephrine. The chemical epinephrine (epi- = “on”; “-nephrine” = kidney) is also known as adrenaline (renal = “kidney”), and norepinephrine is sometimes referred to as noradrenaline. The adrenal gland also produces epinephrine and norepinephrine to be released into the blood stream as hormones, so they can act either as hormones or neurotransmitters.

Cholinergic system: This is the system based on acetylcholine. This includes the neuromuscular junction as an example of a cholinergic synapse, but cholinergic synapses are also found in other parts of the nervous system. They are in the autonomic nervous system, as well as distributed throughout the brain.

Neuropeptides: These are neurotransmitter molecules made up of short chains of amino acids connected by peptide bonds. Some neuropeptides are quite short, such as met-enkephalin, which is five amino acids long. Others are long, such as beta-endorphin, which is 31 amino acids long. Both of these are endorphins (endogenous opioids that have analgesic and pleasure-inducing effects). Neuropeptides are often released at synapses in combination with another neurotransmitter, and they also often act as hormones in other systems of the body. Two important neuropeptides that are released by the posterior pituitary gland, and act as hormones in the body, are oxytocin and vasopressin (the latter is also known as anti-diuretic hormone).

slides.title: Part 5: Neurotransmission
slides.body:
Part 5: Neurotransmission

Effect of neurotransmitters is entirely dependent on type of receptors
e.g., epinephrine and norepinephrine
cause smooth muscle contraction when binding to α adrenergic receptors
reduced blood flow to regions such as GI tract
cause smooth muscle dilation when binding to β adrenergic receptors
increases blood flow to regions such as skeletal muscles and the liver

Adrenergic receptors. Credit: TheCenci786, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
The effect of a neurotransmitter on the postsynaptic element is entirely dependent on the receptor protein. First, if there is no receptor protein in the membrane of the postsynaptic element, then the neurotransmitter has no effect. Second, the depolarizing or hyperpolarizing effect is also dependent on the receptor. 

For example, epinephrine and norepinephrine, which I mentioned are also called adrenaline and noradrenaline (as in this figure), can trigger completely opposite responses in tissues, based on which receptor type is present. As you see, alpha adrenergic receptors cause smooth muscle contraction, while beta adrenergic receptors cause smooth muscle relaxation. This makes sense – when you are in a fight or flight situation, and releasing these hormones, you want to constrict smooth muscle around blood vessels leading to your gastrointestinal system (it is not time to rest and digest). At the same time, you want to dilate blood vessels leading to skeletal muscles (which enable you to either fight or flee) and to the liver (where glycogen is being broken down into glucose for release into the bloodstream, through which it is carried to the brain and skeletal muscles.

slides.title: Part 5: Neurotransmission
slides.body:
Part 5: Neurotransmission

Ionotropic receptors
e.g., nicotinic receptor (acetylcholine) allows an influx of Na+ cations
e.g., glycine receptor allows an influx of Cl- anions

Receptor Types (a) An ionotropic receptor is a channel that opens when the neurotransmitter binds to it. (b) A metabotropic receptor is a complex that causes metabolic changes in the cell when the neurotransmitter binds to it (1). After binding, the G protein hydrolyzes ATP and moves to the effector protein (2). When the G protein contacts the effector protein, the latter is activated. In the case shown, the effector protein then acts on ATP to generate a second messenger, cAMP (3). The second messenger can then go on to cause changes in the neuron, such as opening or closing ion channels, metabolic changes, and changes in gene transcription.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Neurotransmitters bind to one of two classes of receptors at the cell surface, ionotropic or metabotropic. 

Ionotropic receptors are ligand-gated ion channels, such as the nicotinic receptor for acetylcholine, which allows an influx of Na+ cations, or the glycine receptor, which allows an influx of Cl- anions.

slides.title: Part 5: Neurotransmission
slides.body:
Part 5: Neurotransmission

Metabotropic receptor:
G protein-coupled receptor 
(transmembrane receptor protein)
binds NT (the first messenger)
G protein
GTP hydrolase (splits GTP via hydrolysis)
energy used to move to and stimulate/inhibit effector
effector protein
usually an enzyme that catalyzes the generation of a new molecule – a second messenger

Receptor Types (a) An ionotropic receptor is a channel that opens when the neurotransmitter binds to it. (b) A metabotropic receptor is a complex that causes metabolic changes in the cell when the neurotransmitter binds to it (1). After binding, the G protein hydrolyzes ATP and moves to the effector protein (2). When the G protein contacts the effector protein, the latter is activated. In the case shown, the effector protein then acts on ATP to generate a second messenger, cAMP (3). The second messenger can then go on to cause changes in the neuron, such as opening or closing ion channels, metabolic changes, and changes in gene transcription.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes: A metabotropic receptor involves a complex of proteins that result in metabolic changes within the cell. The receptor complex includes the transmembrane receptor protein (a G protein-coupled receptor), a G protein itself, and an effector protein. The neurotransmitter, referred to as the first messenger, binds to the receptor protein on the extracellular surface of the cell, and the intracellular side of the protein initiates activity of the G protein. The G protein is a guanosine triphosphate (GTP) hydrolase that physically moves from the receptor protein to the effector protein to activate the latter. An effector protein is usually an enzyme that catalyzes the generation of a new molecule, which acts as the intracellular mediator of the signal that binds to the receptor. This intracellular mediator is called the second messenger.

slides.title: Part 5: Neurotransmission
slides.body:
Part 5: Neurotransmission

Two main types of second messengers are produced by metabotropic receptors
cAMP by adenylyl cyclase
IP3 and DAG by phospholipase C

Gs-associated G protein-coupled receptor and adenylyl cyclase. Credit: Takanori Nakane, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Gq-associated G protein-coupled receptor and adenylyl cyclase. Credit: Yikrazuul, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes: Different receptors use different second messengers. Two common examples of second messengers are cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) and inositol triphosphate (IP3). The enzyme adenylyl cyclase (an example of an effector protein) makes cAMP; it is stimulated to do so by a Gs (stimulatory) type of G protein. Phospholipase C is the enzyme that makes the second messengers IP3 and DAG; it is stimulated to do so by the Gq category of G protein.

slides.title: Part 5: Neurotransmission
slides.body:
Part 5: Neurotransmission

Various receptor types lead to changes in activation of cell’s enzymes, especially kinases
such activation alters the cell’s metabolic activity & can alter gene transcription
resulting protein changes can alter cell’s function, connection to other cells, and serve as a basis for learning & memory

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024

DNA transcription regulation. Credit: Evrae8, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
slides.notes:
Second messengers, after they are produced by the effector protein, cause metabolic changes within the cell. These changes are most likely the activation of other enzymes in the cell. In neurons, they often modify ion channels, either opening or closing them. 

These enzymes, as well as those activated by the influx of ions or other receptor types, can also cause changes in the cell, such as the alteration of gene expression in the nucleus, and therefore the increased or decreased synthesis of proteins. In neurons, these kinds of changes are often the basis of stronger connections between cells at the synapse and may be the basis of learning and memory.
